source_text:
Ὥσπερ ἄμπελος, μὴ ποιοῦσα καρποὺς καλοὺς,
ἐκκόπτεται ἵνα μὴ τὸν τόπον καταργῇ, οὕτως καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐκριζωθήσεται πᾶς

ὁ μὴ ποιῶν καρποὺς Πνεύματος ἁγίου. Ὡς ἀμήχανον, μὴ βλαβῆναι ἄνθρωπον
κρουσθέντα ὑπὸ βέλους, οὕτως ἀδύνατόν ἐστι, μοναχὸν καταδεξάμενον λογισμὸν
πονηρὸν μὴ τρωθῆναι. Ὥσπερ ὁ ἐξελθὼν ὁδοῦ εὐθείας, πλανᾶται ἐν ἀλλοδαπῇ
χώρᾳ, μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ποῦ πορεύεται, οὕτω καὶ ἄνθρωπος πλανᾶται μὴ πιστεύων εἰς
ὁμοούσιον Τριάδα. Ὥσπερ τις εἰς πολλὰ διαιρούμενος ἕν ἐστι τῇ φύσει, οὕτως καὶ ἡ
ἁγία Τριὰς, εἰ καὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι καὶ ταῖς ὑποστάσεσι διῄρηται, τῇ φύσει μία ἐστί. Θεοῦ
φύσιν οὐ καταλάβοις, οὐδ' εἰ πτεροῖς πετόμενος, ὁ Θεὸς ἀκατάληπτός ἐστι, διὸ καὶ
κτίστης ἡμῶν ἐστιν. Ὥσπερ τὸ κατασκευαζόμενον σκεῦος ἀγνοεῖ τοῦ
κατασκευάσαντος τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ τὴν φύσιν, οὕτω καὶ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δυνήσεται
1
ἐξευρεῖν Θεοῦ φύσιν ἢ ἀρχήν. Τριάδα μὴ περιεργάζου, ἀλλὰ μόνον πίστευε, καὶ
προσκύνει· ὁ γὰρ περιεργαζόμενος οὐ πιστεύει.
Κτήσασθε σοφίαν καὶ μὴ ἀργύριον, ποιήσατε φωτεινὸν ἔνδυμα Χριστοῦ τοῦ
Κυρίου ἡμῶν, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν στολὴν βυσσίνην, ὅτι οὐκ ὠφελήσει ὑπάρχοντα ἐν ἡμέρᾳ
θανάτου. Ὥσπερ πῦρ καταναλίσκει δρυμὸν, οὕτω καταναλωθήσεται πᾶς ἁμαρτωλὸς
ὑπὸ τοῦ αἰωνίου πυρὸς, καὶ οὐ δύναται τελευτῆσαι· ἀθάνατα γὰρ βασανισθήσεται.
thought_title: The vine, the arrow, the Trinity, and the fire
orientation: Evagrius continues his chain of comparisons, now turning to the fate of the fruitless, the wound of an evil thought, the error of not believing in the Trinity one in being, and the eternal fire awaiting sinners.
pass_a_gloss: Just as a vine, not producing good fruits, is cut out so that it may not make the place useless, so also from the Lord will be rooted out every one not producing fruits of the Holy Spirit. As it is impossible for a man not to be harmed when struck by an arrow, so it is impossible for a monk who has accepted an evil thought not to be wounded. Just as the one who has gone out from the straight road wanders in a foreign land, not knowing where he is going, so also a man wanders who does not believe in the Trinity one in being. Just as someone divided into many things is one in nature, so also the holy Trinity, even if it is divided in names and in persons, is one in nature. The nature of God you would not grasp, not even if you fly with wings; God is incomprehensible, and therefore he is also our creator. Just as the vessel being fashioned does not know the beginning and the nature of the one who fashioned it, so also man will not be able to discover the nature or the beginning of God. Do not busy yourself about the Trinity, but only believe, and worship; for the one who busies himself does not believe. Acquire wisdom and not silver, make a shining garment of Christ our Lord, above every linen robe, because possessions will not help in the day of death. Just as fire consumes a thicket, so every sinner will be consumed by the eternal fire, and he cannot die; for he will be tormented immortally.

choices.why: The glossary requires this rendering for the fixed term, preserving the theological sense of one nature.
In this Trinitarian context, hypostases are the distinct persons of the Trinity, matching the brief's statement that the Trinity is divided in names and persons.
The verb means to render idle or ineffective; with τόπον as object, the sense is that the fruitless vine wastes the ground, so 'make the place useless' keeps the literal force.
The verb means to meddle or be overly curious; the brief says the Trinity must be believed and worshipped, not investigated, so this rendering keeps the negative command's force.
Literal rendering of the adjective and noun, preserving the image of a bright robe of Christ.
The adverb ἀθάνατα modifies the passive verb, meaning the torment is without death; this keeps the paradox that the sinner cannot die.
rejected: he will be tortured as an immortal

pass_b_english: Just as a vine that does not produce good fruit is cut out so that it does not make the place useless, so everyone who does not produce the fruits of the Holy Spirit will be rooted out by the Lord. Just as it is impossible for a person struck by an arrow not to be harmed, so it is impossible for a monk who has accepted an evil thought not to be wounded. Just as one who leaves the straight road wanders in a foreign land, not knowing where he is going, so a person who does not believe in the Trinity one in being wanders. Just as something divided into many parts is one in nature, so the Holy Trinity, though divided in names and persons, is one in nature. You could not grasp the nature of God, not even if you flew with wings; God is incomprehensible, and for this reason he is also our Creator. Just as a vessel being made does not know the origin and nature of its maker, so a person will not be able to discover the nature or origin of God. Do not busy yourself about the Trinity, but only believe and worship; for the one who busies himself about it does not believe.

Acquire wisdom and not silver; make for yourselves a shining garment of Christ our Lord, beyond every linen robe, because possessions will not help in the day of death. Just as fire consumes a thicket, so every sinner will be consumed by the eternal fire, and he cannot die; for he will be tormented immortally.

last_rejected.quote: for he will be tormented immortally
last_rejected.why: ἀθάνατα is neuter plural adverbial = 'immortally' or 'for immortality,' but here means 'without end, eternally.' However, 'tormented immortally' is awkward and slightly misleading—soul is immortal, torment is eternal. But 'immortally' as adverb is grammatical. More importantly: the sinner 'cannot die' means in context of eternal punishment, the torment never ends. 'Immortally' is odd English. This is minor at best.
last_rejected.fix: for he will be tormented without end
last_rejected.ruling: ἀθανάτα adverbially modifies βασανισθήσεται; 'tormented immortally' is awkward but within meaning range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: Do not busy yourself about the Trinity
last_rejected.why: περιεργάζου = busy yourself with, be curious about, investigate. 'Busy yourself about' is slightly awkward but conveys sense. 'Do not investigate' or 'do not be curious about' would be clearer. This is minor.
last_rejected.ruling: περιεργάζου means 'busy oneself about/investigate'; rendering is within normal range, just a stylistic preference.

last_rejected.quote: not even if you flew with wings
last_rejected.why: πετόμενος = flying (participle, masculine nominative). Source says 'not even if flying with wings'—the subject is 'you' implied. English 'if you flew with wings' adds 'you' and changes to past subjunctive. This is natural English, not an error.
last_rejected.ruling: πετόμενος is a participle with implied subject; 'if you flew with wings' is natural English for οὐδ' εἰ πτεροῖς πετόμενος, no meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: so everyone who does not produce the fruits of the Holy Spirit will be rooted out by the Lord
last_rejected.source_quote: οὕτως καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐκριζωθήσεται πᾶς ὁ μὴ ποιῶν καρποὺς Πνεύματος ἁγίου
last_rejected.why: Source says 'so from the Lord will be rooted out everyone who does not produce fruits of the Holy Spirit.' English 'rooted out by the Lord'—but source says 'ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου' = 'from the Lord' (source of action, but could mean 'by' in passive). However, 'ἀπό' with passive can mean 'by' (agent). But more precisely, 'rooted out from the Lord' = separated from the Lord? No, ἐκριζόομαι is 'uprooted, rooted out,' and 'ἀπό' indicates the one doing it. Actually in biblical Greek, ὑπό is standard for agent; ἀπό can indicate source/separation. Here 'ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐκριζωθήσεται' likely means 'will be rooted out BY the Lord' (divine judgment). But could it mean 'rooted out FROM the Lord' = separated from the Lord's presence? The context of vine metaphor suggests removal from the vineyard/place. 'ἀπό' with place: 'from the Lord' = away from the Lord. English 'by the Lord' makes God the agent of uprooting; Greek 'ἀπό' suggests separation from God. This is a significant difference: is God doing the uprooting, or is the result being separated from God? In biblical idiom, vines are cut off/removed; 'from the Lord' likely means 'from the Lord's domain.' But 'by the Lord' is a possible interpretation. Let me check: the first clause has 'ἐκκόπτεται' (is cut out) with 'ἵνα μὴ τὸν τόπον καταργῇ' (so as not to make the place useless). The second has 'ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐκριζωθήσεται'—parallel to 'ἐκκόπτεται.' The agent of cutting is implied (the vinedresser/God). 'ἀπό' here is unusual for agent. Actually, looking at this again: 'ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου' most naturally means 'from the Lord' = away from the Lord, i.e., separated from Christ. The English 'by the Lord' changes the meaning: God as active agent vs. removal from God's presence. This is a real issue.
last_rejected.fix: so everyone who does not produce the fruits of the Holy Spirit will be rooted out from the Lord
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπό with passive can mark agent; 'by the Lord' for ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἐκριζωθήσεται is a defensible rendering, not clearly wrong.
